name: BLIS Collective
summary: The BLIS Collective (Black Liberation-Indigenous Sovereignty) is a national Solidarity and Action Hub that sparks collaboration and narrative alignment across Black, Indigenous, and other transformative social movements to advance repair, decolonization, and cultural change. Describing itself as combining the functions of a think tank, cultural studio, regrantor, and movement network, BLIS works through four core areas: narrative research, capacity-building consulting, cultural production, and coalition building.

name: Brave Space Alliance
summary: The first Black-led, trans-led LGBTQ+ center on Chicago's South Side, providing affirming mutual aid, advocacy, and community resources for Black and Brown trans and queer individuals.

name: Bread for the World
summary: Bread for the World is a Christian, nonpartisan advocacy organization headquartered in Washington, DC, urging U.S. policymakers to end hunger domestically and globally.

name: Brighton Park Neighborhood Council (BPNC)
summary: A grassroots community-based nonprofit on Chicago's southwest side that advocates for immigrant rights through legal services, education, rapid response networks, and organizing.

name: CASA Latina
summary: CASA Latina (Consejo de Asentamientos Sustentables de América Latina, or Council of Sustainable Settlements of Latin America) is a regional network that articulates and strengthens national and local networks across Latin America promoting sustainable and regenerative lifestyles. Formed following the 2012 "Call of the Mountain" gathering of ecovillagers in Colombia, CASA connects ecovillages, intentional communities, permaculture and agroecology projects, transition towns, and grassroots NGOs and cooperatives working toward ecological, economic, cultural, and social regeneration.

name: Center for Community Health Equity
summary: Co-founded by DePaul University and Rush University in 2015, this center strives to improve community health outcomes and contribute to the elimination of health inequities in Chicago.

name: Center for Neighborhood Technology (CNT)
summary: A Chicago nonprofit that creates equitable, sustainable, and resilient urban communities through innovative analysis, policy advocacy, and community collaborations on climate and environmental issues.

name: Center for Restorative Justice Works (CRJW)
summary: A grassroots nonprofit founded in 2001 that advocates for and supports children and families of the incarcerated, promoting a restorative justice agenda focused on healing and reconnecting families separated by the criminal justice system.

name: Center for Transformative Action
summary: The Center for Transformative Action (CTA) is an Ithaca, NY–based nonprofit affiliated with Cornell University that provides fiscal sponsorship, incubation, and educational programs to social-change organizations and projects. Founded in 1971 as the Center for Religion, Ethics, and Social Policy to house social justice activism that had grown out of Cornell United Religious Work in the 1960s, the organization adopted its current name in 2009 to reflect a broader mission.

name: Centinela Youth Services
summary: A community-based nonprofit founded in 1975 that has provided diversion and restorative justice work that is trauma-informed for over 40 years across Los Angeles County.

name: Centro de Trabajadores Unidos (United Workers Center)
summary: Member-led, grassroots worker center on Chicago's Southeast Side founded in 2008 by immigrant workers to build worker and immigrant power through labor organizing and collective action.

name: Centro Romero
summary: A community-based organization serving the refugee and immigrant population on Chicago's northeast side through social services, advocacy, and community organizing.

name: Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN)
summary: The Chesapeake Climate Action Network (CCAN) is the oldest and largest grassroots nonprofit dedicated exclusively to fighting climate change in the Chesapeake Bay region of Maryland, Virginia, and Washington, DC. Founded on July 1, 2002 by journalist Mike Tidwell out of his home in Takoma Park, Maryland, with a seed grant from the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, CCAN has grown to a staff of roughly 25 with offices in Takoma Park, Richmond, and Norfolk.

name: Chicago and Midwest Regional Joint Board, Workers United
summary: One of the most active labor unions in the country, representing workers across the Midwest and fighting for living wages, union rights, and an end to right-to-work laws.

name: Chicago Appleseed Center for Fair Courts
summary: Researches and advocates for decarceration and pretrial fairness in Cook County, including helping pass the Illinois Pretrial Fairness Act abolishing cash bail.

name: Chicago Cancer Health Equity Collaborative (ChicagoCHEC)
summary: A National Cancer Institute partnership led by Northwestern University, UIC, and Northeastern Illinois University, advancing cancer health equity through research, education, and community engagement in Chicago.

name: Chicago Coalition to End Homelessness (CCH)
summary: Builds community power and advances racial equity through organizing, advocacy, legal assistance, and education to prevent and end homelessness in Chicago.

name: Chicago Community Bond Fund
summary: Posts bail for people charged with crimes in Cook County who cannot afford it, while organizing for the abolition of money bond and pretrial detention.

name: Chicago Disabilities Fund (Chicago Community Trust)
summary: An affinity fund within the Chicago Community Trust that supports and advises on disability inclusion, rights, and justice across employment, education, and community inclusion.

name: Chicago Environmental Justice Network
summary: A coalition of BIPOC-led, neighborhood-based, grassroots frontline environmental justice organizations working in communities throughout the Chicago metropolitan area, led primarily by women of color on the south and west sides.

name: Chicago Federation of Labor
summary: Umbrella organization for over 320 affiliated unions representing approximately 500,000 union members in Cook County, fighting for organizing, legislative, and political gains for working people.

name: Chicago Food Policy Action Council (CFPAC)
summary: A policy advocacy coalition that co-facilitates and implements policies advancing food justice and food sovereignty in Chicago, with a focus on equitable food access for Black, Indigenous, and communities of color.

name: Chicago Freedom School
summary: A youth-centered organization that provides transformative education and leadership development grounded in racial justice, social movement history, and community organizing.

name: Chicago Housing Initiative (CHI)
summary: A coalition of nine community organizations working to preserve and expand low-cost rental housing and advance racial and economic equity for low-income Chicago renters.

name: Chicago Housing Justice Coalition
summary: A coalition of grassroots organizations fighting for housing justice in Chicago through advocacy, direct action, and the Housing is a Human Right Pledge campaign.

name: Chicago Justice Project
summary: Independent nonprofit research organization that accesses and analyzes data from criminal justice agencies to promote evidence-based reforms serving local community needs.

name: Chicago Laborers' District Council
summary: Represents over 20,000 construction, municipal, and industrial workers across 15 Laborers' Locals in Cook and surrounding counties, with active organizing through the Great Lakes Regional Organizing Committee.

name: Chicago Refugee Coalition
summary: A secular, non-partisan 501(c)3 dedicated to supporting and advocating for refugees through innovative partnerships, community empowerment, and direct service programs.

name: Chicago Region Food System Fund
summary: A philanthropic fund that supports a broad range of food justice organizations, growers, and community groups working to build a resilient and equitable local food system across the Chicago region.

name: Chicago Rehab Network (CRN)
summary: A citywide coalition of over 40 community-based housing development organizations advocating for affordable housing preservation and development since 1977.

name: Chicago United for Equity
summary: An organization that advances racial justice by acknowledging history, shifting power, and building accountability to create a more equitable Chicago.

name: Civicus
summary: CIVICUS: World Alliance for Citizen Participation is a global alliance of civil society organizations and activists working to strengthen citizen action and civil society worldwide. It grew out of a 1991 gathering of 20 civil society leaders from around the world who sought to support citizen participation in governmental decision-making, and was formally founded in 1993, taking its name from the Latin term for "of the community." Originally based in Washington, DC, CIVICUS relocated its global headquarters to Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2002, and now counts more than 17,000 members across over 175 countries.

name: Climate Action Network (CAN)
summary: Climate Action Network (CAN) International is the world's largest network of civil society organizations working on climate change, uniting well over 1,900 member organizations in more than 130 countries, including groups such as Greenpeace and WWF. Founded in 1989, in the same period as the founding of the IPCC, CAN was established to coordinate NGO strategy, share information, and present a unified civil society voice at international climate negotiations.

name: Climate Equity Working Group
summary: The Climate Equity Working Group (CEWG) is an equity-focused coalition of community and advocacy groups organizing for statewide climate justice in Virginia. CEWG's mission centers on contributing to the state's decarbonization while ensuring a just transition for energy workers and fenceline communities, framing its policy work through a racial, economic, geographic, social, and cultural equity lens.

name: Climate Justice Alliance
summary: Climate Justice Alliance (CJA) is a US-based alliance of over 80 community-based, frontline, and movement-support organizations working to build a Just Transition away from an extractive fossil fuel economy toward regenerative, community-controlled local economies. Formed in 2013 after several years of alignment discussions among grassroots climate justice groups, CJA is rooted in the environmental justice movement's history, drawing on foundational documents like the 1991 Principles of Environmental Justice and the 1996 Jemez Principles of Democratic Organizing.

name: Club of Rome
summary: The Club of Rome is a nonprofit think tank and informal network of scientists, economists, business leaders, and current or former heads of state focused on long-term global challenges. It was founded in April 1968 at the Accademia dei Lincei in Rome by Italian industrialist Aurelio Peccei and Scottish scientist Alexander King, who brought together roughly 30 to 36 scientists, industrialists, and civil servants from ten countries to discuss what Peccei termed the "world problematique": the interlinked crises of environmental degradation, poverty, resource depletion, and unchecked industrial growth.

name: Communities United
summary: A survivor-led, intergenerational racial justice organization in Chicago that builds grassroots leadership and advocates for youth empowerment, housing equity, education equity, and restorative justice.

name: Confluence Rising (formerly California Conference for Equality and Justice / CCEJ)
summary: A Southern California nonprofit active since the 1950s that runs a Restorative Youth Diversion Program as an alternative to incarceration, and was among the first to promote restorative justice practices in LA County schools.

name: Convivialist International
summary: Convivialist International is a loosely organized global network of intellectuals and activists advancing "convivialism," a humanist civic and political philosophy centered on principles for living together cooperatively, sustainably, and without the domination of neoliberalism, productivism, or populism. The movement originated from discussions beginning in Tokyo in July 2010, and produced its first text, the Convivialist Manifesto: A Declaration of Interdependence, published in French in 2013 and signed by 64 predominantly French-speaking authors.

name: Crianza Mutua Colombia
summary: Crianza Mutua Colombia is one of the founding "weaver" networks of the Global Tapestry of Alternatives (GTA), working to identify, document, and connect grassroots communities and collectives ("entramados comunitarios") in Colombia that are dismantling hierarchical social structures and building autonomy from state and market systems. The term "crianza mutua" (mutual upbringing or mutual nurturing) draws on an Andean Indigenous concept describing the caring, reciprocal relationship between people and all beings around them—plants, animals, mountains, and community.

name: Crianza Mutua México
summary: Crianza Mutua México is one of the founding "weaver" networks of the Global Tapestry of Alternatives (GTA), operating in Mexico (alongside a parallel process in Colombia) to identify, document, and connect grassroots "entramados comunitarios" (communal webs) that are dismantling hierarchies and building autonomy from market and state systems in everyday life. Inspired by Zapatismo, the process emerged within the autonomous Universidad de la Tierra in Oaxaca, co-founded by intellectuals Gustavo Esteva and Arturo Escobar, who began identifying and documenting community initiatives that challenge the dominant economic system.

name: Crossroads Antiracism Organizing and Training
summary: An organization that partners with Chicago-area institutions to transform their cultures and practices toward racial justice through antiracism organizing, training, and policy development.

name: Crossroads Fund
summary: A public foundation founded in 1981 that supports grassroots community organizations working on racial, social, and economic justice throughout the Chicago area.

name: DC Bar Foundation – DCSJTN
summary: The DC Social Justice Transformations Network (DCSJTN) is a Washington, DC coalition convened by the DC Bar Foundation to reimagine and improve the District's civil legal aid system through an anti-racist, anti-poverty, user-centered lens. It emerged from an initial convening in June 2021, when the Foundation brought together nearly 60 legal aid providers, funders, community activists, social service providers, government actors, and technology experts; it was originally named the DC Legal Aid Transformations Network before being renamed in 2023 to better reflect its broadening scope and inclusivity.

name: DC Greens
summary: DC Greens is a Washington, DC nonprofit, founded in 2009, that advances health equity by building a just and resilient local food system. The organization places racial justice and health equity at the center of its work, partnering with residents, community advocates, clinics, farms, grocery retailers, and DC government agencies across all eight wards.

name: Deep Transformation Network
summary: The Deep Transformation Network (DTN) is a global online community, founded and hosted by author Jeremy Lent (The Patterning Instinct, The Web of Meaning), exploring pathways toward a life-affirming, ecologically regenerated future. Originating from a community of readers drawn to Lent's writing, the network has since grown to several thousand members worldwide (with figures reported between roughly 3,500 and 5,000 members in recent years) who engage in an active discussion feed, live monthly events with expert panels, and self-organized peripheral subnetworks.

name: Democracy without Borders
summary: Democracy Without Borders (DWB) is an international nongovernmental organization, established in 2017 with a legal seat in Berlin and national chapters worldwide, that advocates for global democracy, global governance, and global citizenship. The organization is the successor to the Committee for a Democratic UN (KDUN), founded in Berlin in 2003 to promote UN democratization through parliamentary representation of the world's citizens; DWB's members voted to adopt the new name and broader mandate in February 2017.

name: Disability Inclusion of Greater Kansas City (Disability:IN GKC)
Disability Lead
summary: A Chicago-based nonprofit building a deeper bench of leaders with disabilities to serve on boards, commissions, and civic roles to advance disability justice.

name: Disability Rights Action Coalition for Housing (DRACH)
summary: A grassroots organizing coalition under Access Living that fights for accessible, affordable housing for people with disabilities through direct advocacy and community education in Chicago.

name: Elevate (formerly Elevate Energy)
summary: A Chicago-headquartered nonprofit working nationally to create a just and equitable world by expanding access to clean, affordable energy, heat, and water in underserved homes and communities.

name: Enlace Chicago
summary: A grassroots community organization in Little Village that trains and employs community health workers to promote holistic wellness, prevent chronic disease, and expand access to healthcare for residents.

name: Equip for Equality
summary: Illinois's federally designated protection and advocacy organization providing legal services, self-advocacy assistance, and disability rights education statewide.

name: Equity and Transformation (EAT)
summary: Community-led nonprofit founded by and for post-incarcerated people, organizing Black informal workers in Chicago around criminal justice reform and economic equity.

name: Erie Neighborhood House
summary: A social service agency working primarily with low-income immigrant families across multiple Chicago neighborhoods, providing education, legal services, and community support.

name: Esperanza Health Centers
summary: A Federally Qualified Health Center operating multiple clinics on Chicago's Southwest Side, providing bilingual primary care and wellness services to primarily Latino underserved communities regardless of ability to pay.

name: EverThrive Illinois
summary: A nonprofit advancing health equity and reproductive justice in Illinois for nearly 40 years, focusing on access to quality healthcare for women, children, and families most impacted by injustice.

name: Eviction Defense Coalition (Right to Counsel Program)
Faith in Place
summary: An environmental nonprofit based in Chicago that works with interfaith communities across Illinois, Indiana, and Wisconsin to educate, connect, and advocate for climate justice and healthier communities.

name: Family Resource Center on Disabilities
summary: Established in 1969, FRCD is Chicago's federally funded Parent Training and Information Center empowering families of children with disabilities to advocate for education rights.

name: Gardeneers
summary: A Chicago nonprofit providing full-service school garden programs on the South and West Sides, connecting students to fresh food and addressing root causes of food inequality through youth-led education.

name: Getting Grown Collective
summary: A multigenerational collective striving to equip Black and Brown communities with tools for food and land sovereignty, operating multiple gardens and coordinating Black and Brown Farmers' Exchanges.

name: Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature
Global Gardens Chicago (Global Garden Refugee Training Farm)
summary: An Albany Park urban farm supporting refugee families who grow organic vegetables for home consumption and sale, building food security and economic opportunity for newly arrived refugees.

name: Global Platform for the Right to the City
Grassroots Collaborative
summary: A community-labor coalition of over 150,000 Illinois residents that builds power with working families through organizing and advocacy for racial justice and economic equity.

name: Greater Chicago Food Depository
summary: Chicago's central food bank, operating a network of over 800 partner pantries and programs across Cook County while advocating for anti-hunger policy and addressing root causes of food insecurity including structural racism.

name: Harmony Arts Collective
summary: Community arts organization promoting creativity and cultural exchange.

name: Health & Disability Advocates
summary: A Chicago nonprofit that builds federal, state, and local policies promoting economic and healthcare security for people with disabilities and low-income older adults.

name: Health & Medicine Policy Research Group (HMPRG)
summary: An independent policy center founded in 1981 that conducts research, advocacy, and coalition building to advance social justice and health equity in Illinois.

name: Healthy Communities Foundation
summary: A health conversion foundation that allocates the majority of its funding to community-led organizations addressing health inequities in Chicago and the western suburbs of Cook County.

name: Homeboy Industries
summary: The world's largest gang rehabilitation and re-entry program, providing training, support, and restorative community for formerly gang-involved and previously incarcerated individuals in Los Angeles.

name: Housing Action Illinois
summary: A 200-member statewide coalition headquartered in Chicago that advances housing justice and equitable housing policy across Illinois through organizing, advocacy, and member support.

name: Illinois AFL-CIO
summary: State federation representing nearly 1 million Illinois labor movement members, with Chicago headquarters, advocating for working families through organizing, political mobilization, and legislative action.

name: Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights (ICIRR)
summary: A statewide nonprofit coalition that advocates for the rights of immigrants and refugees through public policy advocacy, community organizing, and leadership development.

name: Illinois Environmental Council (IEC)
summary: A statewide coalition that builds the power of the environmental community by convening and advocating on behalf of more than 150 member organizations working to protect the Illinois environment, including on climate justice.

name: Illinois Food Justice Alliance
summary: An intergenerational, multicultural coalition co-led by CFPAC, HEAL Food Alliance, and Illinois Stewardship Alliance, working to build a just and equitable statewide food system with deep roots in Chicago.

name: Impact for Equity
summary: Policy advocacy organization working to reduce Illinois' prison population, advance the SAFE-T Act, and eliminate racial disparities across all phases of the criminal legal system.

name: Inner-City Muslim Action Network (IMAN)
summary: Community organization fostering health, wellness, and healing in Chicago's inner city by organizing for social change, including reentry support for formerly incarcerated individuals.

name: Jewish Council on Urban Affairs (JCUA)
summary: A nonprofit founded in 1964 that mobilizes the Jewish community to advance racial and economic justice through grassroots organizing, youth education, and community development.

name: John Howard Association of Illinois
summary: Illinois' only independent nonprofit citizen correctional oversight organization, monitoring all state prisons and advocating for humane, transparent, and reformed carceral conditions.

name: Latino Union of Chicago
summary: Founded in 2000, organizes at the intersection of immigration and labor justice, collaborating with low-income immigrant and U.S.-born day laborers and domestic workers to improve social and economic conditions.

name: Law Center for Better Housing (LCBH)
summary: The only nonprofit law firm in Chicago focused solely on low- and moderate-income renters, providing free legal services, eviction defense, and housing policy advocacy.

name: Lawndale Christian Health Center (LCHC)
summary: A community-based Federally Qualified Health Center founded in 1984, providing quality affordable primary care to eliminate health disparities in Lawndale and neighboring West Side communities.

name: Lawndale Christian Legal Center
summary: The only community-based legal practice in Chicago dedicated to the felony criminal defense of children and emerging adults in the Lawndale neighborhood.

name: Live Free Illinois
summary: Runs a Decarceration Fellowship for recently returning citizens, training them as community leaders to challenge punitive criminal justice policies and drive reform.

name: Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities (MOPD)
summary: Chicago's city office dedicated to fostering accessibility, equal opportunities, and full participation for residents with disabilities through direct services, policy, and public education.

name: Mental Health America of the Heartland
Metropolitan Tenants Organization (MTO)
summary: Founded in 1981, MTO educates, organizes, and empowers tenants to exercise their right to affordable and safe housing through a free renters' rights hotline and building organizing.

name: Midwest Environmental Justice Network (MWEJN)
summary: A regional network based in Chicago supporting frontline community organizations across the Midwest in advocating for energy justice, pollution reduction, and equitable clean energy transitions.

name: Millennium Alliance for Humanity and the Biosphere
Mujeres Latinas en Acción
summary: A Pilsen-based nonprofit empowering Latinas and immigrant women through culturally responsive services including domestic violence support, counseling, legal advocacy, and community outreach.

name: National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC)
summary: Provides free legal consultations and representation for low-income immigrants, with a focus on deportation defense, asylum seekers, and unaccompanied minors.

name: Neighbors for Environmental Justice (N4EJ)
summary: A southwest side Chicago organization that educates, advocates, and organizes for environmental justice, recognizing that environmental justice cannot be separated from racial justice.

name: Northwest Center Chicago
summary: Partners with the Chicago Legal Protection Fund and ICIRR to develop immigrant leaders, provide Know Your Rights education, and grow community power in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood.

name: Nourishing Hope
summary: One of Chicago's largest and longest-operating food pantries, providing food access, mental health counseling, and social services to neighbors across the city with a dignity-centered approach.

name: ONE Northside
summary: A mixed-income, multi-ethnic intergenerational organization uniting diverse communities on Chicago's North Side to eliminate injustice through bold grassroots community organizing and leadership development.

name: Openlands
summary: A Chicago-based land conservation nonprofit that partners with environmental justice organizations on urban forestry, green space access, and community greening to address neighborhood climate change concerns.

name: Palenque LSNA (formerly Logan Square Neighborhood Association)
summary: A community-based organization building power for housing equity in Logan Square, Avondale, and Hermosa through anti-displacement campaigns, community land trusts, and housing ordinance advocacy.

name: People for Community Recovery (PCR)
summary: A south side Chicago organization advocating for frontline communities on the environmental and climate crisis, working to ensure residents are at the forefront of the growing clean energy economy in Illinois.

name: Pilsen Alliance
summary: A grassroots social justice organization developing working-class leadership and fighting gentrification and displacement through tenant organizing and housing justice campaigns in Pilsen.

name: Pilsen Environmental Rights and Reform Organization (P.E.R.R.O.)
summary: A grassroots community group of Pilsen residents founded in 2004 that fights the disproportionate amount of pollution in Pilsen through environmental justice advocacy and a just transition framework.

name: Pilsen Housing Cooperative (PIHCO)
summary: A limited-equity, scattered-site housing cooperative founded in 2017 by longtime Pilsen residents to combat gentrification and expand community-controlled affordable homeownership.

name: Precious Blood Ministry of Reconciliation
summary: Builds relationships among youth and families impacted by violence, creates safe spaces for healing, and promotes restorative justice approaches to conflict on Chicago's South Side.

name: Progress Center for Independent Living
summary: A community-based Center for Independent Living founded in 1988, serving the Chicago metro area by providing tools, advocacy, and systems-change work for people with disabilities.

name: Puerto Rican Cultural Center (PRCC)
summary: A community-based, activist-oriented organization in Humboldt Park providing health, educational, and cultural services grounded in self-determination for Puerto Rican and Latino communities.

name: Respiratory Health Association
summary: A Chicago nonprofit fighting lung disease and promoting health equity through research, advocacy, and community-based programs targeting populations with disproportionate rates of asthma and lung disease.

name: Restore Justice Foundation
summary: Advocates for people serving Illinois' most extreme sentences, focusing on sentencing reform, prison conditions, and pathways to release while centering system-impacted voices.

name: Safer Foundation
summary: One of the nation's largest nonprofits focused on employment, education, and reentry support for people with criminal records, headquartered in Chicago since 1972.

name: Sinai Urban Health Institute (SUHI)
summary: A nationally recognized research institute at Sinai Chicago that partners with community members and organizations to document disparities and build health equity on Chicago's West Side.

name: South Side Healthy Community Organization (SSHCO)
summary: A nonprofit coalition of 13 healthcare providers committed to improving health outcomes and building health equity across 15 zip codes on Chicago's South Side.

name: Southeast Environmental Task Force (SETF)
summary: A nonprofit founded in 1989 serving the southeast side and south suburbs of Chicago through environmental education, pollution prevention, and sustainable development in an area with a long history of industrial pollution.

name: Southside Together Organizing for Power (STOP)
summary: A South Side community organization building resident power to fight gentrification, displacement, and racial and economic injustice through organizing and popular education.

name: The Arc of Illinois
summary: The largest statewide advocacy organization for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities in Illinois, with significant organizing presence in the Chicago region.

name: The Arc of the Ozarks - Kansas City Division
The Decarceration Collective
summary: Woman-powered law office and advocacy collective fighting to free people unjustly sentenced to life in prison for drugs and to dismantle the policies behind mass incarceration.

name: The Resurrection Project (TRP)
summary: Leads the Chicago Legal Protection Fund's Community Navigator Program, training community leaders to conduct Know Your Rights workshops and prevent deportations.

name: UNITE HERE Local 1
summary: Chicago-based union local organizing hospitality workers and leading battles for workers' rights, immigration reform, living wages, and quality jobs across the Chicago area.

name: Urban Growers Collective
summary: A Black-led nonprofit operating eight urban farms primarily on Chicago's South and West Sides, growing fresh produce and offering youth job training, education, and leadership development programs.

name: Urban Peace Institute (UPI)
summary: A Los Angeles-based nonprofit dedicated to reducing violence and building community safety by training credible messengers in restorative justice and trauma-informed care, and advocating for alternatives to mass incarceration.

name: Urban Youth Network
summary: Nonprofit organization supporting urban youth through education and mentorship programs.

name: Warehouse Workers for Justice
summary: Worker center founded in 2009 to win stable, living wage jobs for logistics and distribution workers in the Chicagoland and Will County area, the largest intermodal hub in the U.S.

name: West Side United
summary: A multi-sector collaborative of hospitals, community organizations, and partners working to reduce the life expectancy gap and advance health and economic equity in 10 West Side neighborhoods.

name: Western Justice Center
summary: A leader in conflict resolution education for nearly 40 years, partnering with K-12 schools across Greater Los Angeles to implement restorative practices as trauma-informed alternatives to punitive discipline.

name: Woods Fund Chicago
summary: A grantmaking foundation committed to racial and economic justice by funding community organizing and public policy advocacy centered on communities of color across Chicago.

name: Workers Center for Racial Justice
summary: A grassroots organization fighting for Black liberation that organizes Black workers and families to address unemployment, low-wage work, and over-criminalization through direct action and policy advocacy.

name: World Assembly of Struggles and Resistance of the WSF
YES to Life No to Mining Network
Youth Justice Coalition (YJC)
summary: A Los Angeles-based nonprofit devoted to challenging race, gender, and class inequality in California's juvenile and criminal justice systems through direct action, policy advocacy, and community organizing.
